4. Whether "healthy family members" relatives belong in scope (I included them as relatives).

You are an extraction helper for the GP-RareLink research study (literature curation; no patient data beyond what the published paper contains).
Follow /home/user/gp-rarelink/pipeline/extract/claude_code/prompts/extract_v6.md exactly. It tells you to read the schema /home/user/gp-rarelink/pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json and the rules /home/user/gp-rarelink/pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md.
Paper: /home/user/gp-rarelink/data/literature/ha20/fulltext_md/35155270.md
Output file: /home/user/gp-rarelink/data/extracted/ha20/ow-ha20/per_paper/35155270.json
Private scratch directory (the only place for temporary files): /tmp/openweight_scratch/ow-ha20/35155270
Hard limits: read only the paper, the schema, the rules and the instructions file. Do not open any other repository file, do not use web search or web fetch, do not run git, and write nowhere except your output file and your scratch directory. Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its patients, the gene or the variants.
Reply in under 200 words: rows per table, number of individuals, whether reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant is true (the schema defines this field for this disease), and at most five of the most important uncertainties.
I'll start by reading the instructions, schema, and rules files.

1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163

165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

1	Extraction rules (GP-RareLink, v1). These rules apply to every table and every row.
2	
3	1. Use only the supplied document. Do not use outside knowledge about the gene, the disease, specific variants or specific patients. If the document does not state something, the value is "not reported" (for text fields) or null (for numeric and date fields). Never fill a gap from memory.
4	2. Every value must be supported by a verbatim quote copied exactly from the document. Do not paraphrase inside the quote. If no exact quote supports a value, do not emit the value.
5	3. Keep original strings. Record variant descriptions, ages, feature names and labels exactly as printed. Never convert protein-only variant descriptions into cDNA notation, never add a transcript that is not printed, never translate units.
6	4. Three-state phenotypes: a feature is "observed" only when the document says the person has or had it, and "excluded" only when the document explicitly says it was absent, negative or not found in that person. Silence is "not reported". Never turn silence into "excluded".
7	5. One row per real person per document. Relatives described in the document are their own rows with is_proband = false unless the document calls them probands. Do not merge people, and do not create a person the document does not describe.
8	6. Cohort tables: when a table lists many patients, extract each patient row separately with the table's own patient identifier as individual_label_in_paper. Keep the row-to-column alignment of the table; when a cell is empty or marked "-", "NA" or "ND", treat it as not reported.
9	7. Re-reports: if the document says that any of its patients were described in an earlier publication, record that statement and the citation in the publications table. Do not drop the patient.
10	8. Do not infer inheritance or zygosity. "de novo" requires that the document states parental testing showed the variant absent in both parents. "heterozygous" requires that the document says so or the gene is described as monoallelic for that person.
11	9. Prefer "not reported" to a plausible guess. Abstention is correct behaviour.

8	# Dysregulation of the Intestinal Microbiome in Patients With Haploinsufficiency of A20
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	IntroductionHaploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a form of inborn errors of immunity (IEI). IEIs are genetically occurring diseases, some of which cause intestinal dysbiosis. Due to the dysregulation of regulatory T cells (Tregs) observed in patients with HA20, gut dysbiosis was associated with Tregs in intestinal lamina propria.MethodsStool samples were obtained from 16 patients with HA20 and 15 of their family members. Infant samples and/or samples with recent antibiotics use were excluded; hence, 26 samples from 13 patients and 13 family members were analyzed. The 16S sequencing process was conducted to assess the microbial composition of samples. Combined with clinical information, the relationship between the microbiome and the disease activity was statistically analyzed.ResultsThe composition of gut microbiota in patients with HA20 was disturbed compared with that in healthy family members. Age, disease severity, and use of immunosuppressants corresponded to dysbiosis. However, other explanatory factors, such as abdominal symptoms and probiotic treatment, were not associated. The overall composition at the phylum level was stable, but some genera were significantly increased or decreased. Furthermore, among the seven operational taxonomic units (OTUs) that increased, two OTUs, Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus salivarius, considerably increased in patients with autoantibodies than those without autoantibodies.DiscussionDetailed interaction on intestinal epithelium remains unknown; the relationship between the disease and stool composition change helps us understand the mechanism of an immunological reaction to microorganisms.
13	
14	## Introduction
15	
16	A20, which is encoded by the tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) gene, is a negative regulator of the TNF-nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway. Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) causes autoinflammatory and autoimmune disorders (Kadowaki et al., 2018). Dysbiosis of the intestinal microbiome has been observed in some inborn errors of immunities (IEIs)/primary immunodeficiency disease, such as chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) (Sokol et al., 2016), X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis (XIAP) deficiency (Sokol et al., 2016; Ono et al., 2021), tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A (TTC7A) deficiency (Sokol et al., 2016), common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) (Jørgensen et al., 2016; Varricchi et al., 2021), and Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite IEIs having a monogenetic nature, they vary in severity relating to the microbiome (Liu et al., 2021). Little is known about the mechanism of dysbiosis in patients with IEI, but the association of gut microbiota and regulatory T cells (Tregs) was reported (Liu et al., 2021). Tregs regulate A20 (Kadowaki et al., 2020); as a result, the gut microbiota of patients with HA20 plays a vital role in association with Tregs. Alternatively, the mouse lacking A20 expression in dendritic cells showed intestinal dysbiosis (Talpin et al., 2019). This is the first report of the microbiome in patients with HA20.
17	
18	## Materials and Methods
19	
20	### Research Participants and Samples
21	
22	Kadowaki et al. (2018) previously reported that there were 22 patients with HA20 from nine families in Japan. Thirty-six individuals from nine families, including 18 patients, 17 healthy family members living together, and a sibling whose genetic information is unknown, agreed to participate in this study. Next, fecal samples were obtained from 16 patients and 15 healthy relatives from eight corresponding families. Clinical characteristics of the patients were previously reported (patients 3–5, 7–13, and 17–22), and additional information, such as sex, age at the sample collection, symptoms, and medication, was collected (Supplementary Table 1).
23	
24	### The Classification of the Disease Severity of Haploinsufficiency of A20
25	
26	We proposed the classification of disease severity for clinical manifestations of patients with HA20. The mild type was defined as asymptomatic or minor phenotype (e.g., mild recurrent stomatitis and/or rash). The moderate type was defined as paroxysmal symptoms (e.g., recurrent fever and/or abdominal pain). The frequency of symptoms is once or more for at least 3 months. The severe type was defined as persistent inflammation (e.g., fever, central nerve lesion, vascular lesion, ocular lesion, intestinal lesion, and/or arthritis) sustained over 2 weeks.
27	
28	### Detection of the Microbiome
29	
30	Fecal samples were collected and stored at 4°C under anaerobic conditions until preparation. Fecal samples were stirred until completely homogenized and suspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) containing 20% glycerol (1 g of feces per 5 ml) and poured through a filter to remove large-sized food-derived debris. The fecal suspension was added to EDTA (final concentration of 10 mM, Nacalai) and stored at −80°C until use. After thawing, 100 μl of fecal suspension was gently mixed and incubated in 800 μl of TE10 (10 mM of Tris-HCl and 10 mM of EDTA) buffer containing RNase A (final concentration of 100 μg/ml, Invitrogen) and lysozyme (final concentration of 15 mg/ml, Sigma) for 1 h at 37°C. Purified achromopeptidase (final concentration of 2,000 U/ml, Wako) was added and further incubated for 30 min at 37°C. Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) (final concentration of 1%) and proteinase K (final concentration of 1 mg/ml, Roche) were further added to the mixture and incubated for 1 h at 55°C. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted with phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1 at pH 7.9), precipitated with isopropanol (equal volume to the aqueous phase), washed with 1 ml of 70% ethanol, and gently resuspended in 30 μl of TE buffer. We used 40 ng of DNA per sample for the sequence.
31	
32	The sequencing of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene from fecal samples was performed as previously described (Kim et al., 2013; Kakihana et al., 2016). The hypervariable V1–2 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified by PCR using barcoded 27Fmod and 338R primers. DNA extracted from Escherichia coli Strain SE 11 (isolated from a healthy adult) was used as the positive control template, whereas a DNA-free sample was used as the negative control. The electrophoresis procedure confirmed the PCR amplicons and negative reaction. Then, an equal amount of purified PCR amplicons was sequenced on a MiSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA). Next, 3,000 high-quality reads were randomly selected per sample and analyzed to minimize the overestimation of species richness during clustering associated with the sequencing error (Kim et al., 2013). Good’s coverage index (Singleton et al., 2001) for the 3,000 reads per sample in the current study was 0.980, indicating a high degree of coverage and a sufficient read number for the fecal microbiome analysis. Furthermore, the reads were sorted into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) using the UCLUST algorithm, at a sequence identity threshold of 97% (Stackebrandt and Goebel, 1994; Konstantinidis and Tiedje, 2005). Taxonomic assignments of each OTU were made by similarity searching against the publicly available 16S (RDP v.10.27 and CORE) and National Center for Biotechnology Information genome database, using GLSEARCH. OTU-based microbial diversity was estimated using the Shannon index with Scikit-bio (v.0.5.5). A comparison of each group (family, HA20) in the unweighted and weighted UniFrac principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was evaluated by using permutational multivariate ANOVA (PERMANOVA) with Scikit-bio (v.0.5.5) (Anderson, 2017).
33	
34	### Statistical Analysis
35	
36	Statistical analysis of OTUs and Shannon index was performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Values are represented as median (minimum–maximum). The threshold for significance was p < 0.05. Also, stratified analysis was performed using the two-tailed t-test for ordinal scale or regression analysis for continuous scale. Statistical analyses were conducted using R package (exactRankTests) or JMP Pro v.16.0.0 (SAS Institute Inc., NC, USA). The linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) method was performed on the Huttenhower lab Galaxy server (https://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/galaxy/) by importing the bacterial relative abundance values at the genus level with Kruskal–Wallis test p < 0.05 and LDA score (log10) > 2 (Segata et al., 2011).
37	
38	## Results
39	
40	Thirty-one fecal samples from 16 patients and 15 healthy family members were sequenced. However, samples from three patients who received antibiotic treatment within 4 weeks of stool collection were excluded from statistical analysis. Also, two samples from children under the age of 3 years were excluded from statistical analysis because their gut microbiome is naturally different from the older’s microbiome (Yatsunenko et al., 2012). Nobody but an excluded younger brother (P22-sib) has food allergies. The median (min–max) age of 13 patients with HA20 and their healthy family members of 13 individuals were 19 (3–43) and 36 (4–49) years (p = 0.09, Wilcoxon rank-sum test), respectively. Patients with HA20 consist of four mild, four moderate, and five severe patients. Eleven of 13 patients and eight of 13 presented with stomatitis and abdominal symptoms, respectively. One patient was treated with probiotics and 5 with immunosuppressants (Supplementary Table 1).
41	
42	Ten thousand reads were used from an average (and SD) of 53,935 (± 9,383) raw reads. An average of 9,848 reads passed the filter, and every 3,000 Passed Filter reads were used for OTU analysis. The number of OTUs in patients’ samples was considerably less than their healthy members (median 123 vs. 150, p = 0.049, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) (Figure 1A). Likewise, the Shannon index in patients’ samples was significantly less than their healthy members (median 4.68 vs. 5.26, p = 0.009, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) (Figure 1B), whereas the principal component analysis showed a significant difference in the composition of the intestinal microbiome in unweighted UniFrac analysis (p = 0.008, PERMANOVA) (Figure 2A), although not significant in weighted UniFrac analysis (p = 0.059) (Figure 2B). Thus, the stratified analysis suggested that any sex, stomatitis, abdominal symptoms, and use of probiotics do not affect the microbiome diversity (Tables 1 and 2). Lower age was significantly associated with a lower Shannon index although insignificantly with OTUs. Both disease severity and immunosuppressant use were associated with a lower number of OTUs with significance, and they showed lower Shannon index although not significantly.

75	
76	At the phylum level, there was no significant difference between patients with HA20 and their family members (Figure 3 and Supplementary Table 2). Conversely, at the genus level, five genera (Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, Butyricicoccus, Haemophilus, and Enterococcus) increased, and another four (Ruminococcus, Clostridium, Parabacteroides, and Alistipes) decreased in patients with HA20 compared with their family members (LDA score greater than two at p < 0.05 with LEfSe analysis) (Figure 4A). At the OTU level, seven OTUs significantly increased in patients with HA20 compared with their family members (p < 0.001: closest species/strain name Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Streptococcus mutans, and Veillonella sp. oral taxon 158, p < 0.05: Bifidobacterium dentium, Lactobacillus salivarius, Enterococcus avium, and Eubacterium eligens, Wilcoxon rank-sum test). Most of these OTUs are indigenous bacteria and are undetected in the intestinal microbiota. As a representative, only one of two healthy child siblings under 10 years and none of 11 healthy adult members had H. parainfluenzae, when all six child patients with HA20 and two of seven adult patients with HA20 had it (Figure 4B). None of these seven OTUs showed a significant correlation with either stomatitis or abdominal symptoms. However, two of seven OTUs showed a significant difference between patients with and without autoantibodies (four and five patients, respectively; four patients were not analyzed) (Figure 4C).

82	## Discussion
83	
84	This study demonstrated that patients with HA20 show intestinal dysbiosis. Despite HA20 being a genetically occurring disease, previous studies report bacterial composition changes in other IEIs. XIAP deficiency is a rare IEI, and it is characterized by recurrent hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and refractory inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) similar to Crohn’s disease. Furthermore, patients with XIAP deficiency showed intestinal dysbiosis and IBD, which are rescued by allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (Ono et al., 2021). These data further establish the hypothesis that monogenic disease is the cause of gut dysbiosis. From previous studies, there are 118 of 354 IEIs that exhibit gastrointestinal symptoms (Hartono et al., 2019), and the interaction between bacteria and the immune system might vary with the disease. For instance, immunoglobulin A secreted at the mucosal surface of the gastrointestinal tract was associated with selective IgA deficiency (Berbers et al., 2019), and the absence of various subsets of T cells in intestinal lamina propria was associated with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (Clarke et al., 2018).
85	
86	The mechanism that causes dysbiosis in patients with HA20 is mediated by Tregs because it is a key factor of immunoregulatory disorders in patients with HA20 (Liu et al., 2021), and in the mouse model of Treg-associated monogenic autoimmune disorders, Aire knockout mouse showed significant dysbiosis (Dobeš et al., 2015). Mouse models, Aire-deficient mice (Gray et al., 2007), and Foxp3 knockout mice (Chinen et al., 2010) exhibit an autoimmune phenotype even in germ-free conditions, and it was concluded that these diseases are independent of commensal microbial regulation (Liu et al., 2021). Conversely, the Treg-depleted model showed more severe inflammation in the small intestine of specific pathogen-free mice than germ-free mice, which indicates that the disease severity is associated with the microbiome (Liu et al., 2021). These findings indicate the possible association between disease severity and gut dysbiosis. Additionally, data from this study showed a significant correlation between disease severity and dysbiosis. The use of immunosuppressants, an alternative indicator of disease severity, also correlated with dysbiosis.
87	
88	Another possible mechanism of dysbiosis is metabolism. A mouse model lacking A20 in specific dendritic cells reported aberrant expression of antibacterial peptides and luminal dysbiosis (Talpin et al., 2019).
89	
90	Ten of 18 patients with HA20 were treated with immunosuppressants (Kadowaki et al., 2020), and one refractory patient successfully received hematopoietic cell transplantation (Shiraki et al., 2021). However, less invasive therapy would be required. Successful fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is reported in patients with HIV (Serrano-Villar et al., 2021) and the mouse model of Behcet’s disease (Ye et al., 2018), while there is no evidence of FMT in patients with IEIs including HA20. Further study is required to clarify the mechanism of dysbiosis in patients with HA20 and IEIs, to determine the biomarker of the disease, and to discover if FMT works or not.
91	
92	Several monogenic IEIs inform us how the disease-specific immune dysfunction causes disease-specific dysbiosis. Collectively, we can easily understand how the complex immune systems respond to various microorganisms. This study showed that S. mutans and L. salivarius significantly increased in both patients with HA20, those with autoantibodies compared with family members and patients without autoantibodies, respectively. Since the sample size was small for statistical analysis (13 vs. 13, and 4 vs. 5, respectively), statistical significance in two manners was rare enough to reject the null hypothesis. Also, although the close mechanism remains unclear, it was suggested that these two OTUs might be associated with autoimmune onset.
93	
94	In the context of statistical analysis, we excluded patients younger than 3 years and/or patients with antibiotics use because they present a confounding bias for microbiota (Hopkins et al., 2002; Yatsunenko et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2020). However, our data suggested that lower age is the explanatory variable for lower Shannon index, not for OTU numbers. This potential confounding bias is statistically a problem but not clinically crucial. Considering clinical management, both lower age and antibiotics use affect disease severity as well as microbiome diversity. Indeed, the excluded patients based on antibiotics use [previously described as P4, P9, and P21 (Kadowaki et al., 2018)] were relatively younger (4, 1, and 3 years old, respectively) and more severe (P4 and P9 are moderate; P21 is severe) than the included patients. Early-onset patients could be regarded as more strongly influenced by genetics and so potentially more severe than late-onset patients.
95	
96	This study has several limitations. Firstly, clinical heterogeneity exists among medications, such as probiotics and antibiotics. The potential confounding factor is underestimated because of the small sample size. Secondly, because of rare diseases, it is difficult to collect more fecal samples for statistical analysis of the potential confounding factor described. Multivariate analysis was unfeasible due to small samples. Thirdly, not all patients with HA20 received gastrointestinal endoscopy, and so alternative indicators such as the disease severity or abdominal symptoms do not necessarily reflect the exact intestinal condition.
97	
98	## Concluding Remarks
99	
100	We investigated the intestinal microbiome composition in patients with HA20 and identified that seven OTUs significantly increased in the patients. In particular, S. mutans and L. salivarius significantly increased in patients with HA20 and autoantibodies, and these OTUs were associated with autoimmune onset.

"method_note": "Table transcription: Supplementary Table 1 (16 patients, 15 relatives) and the text were read directly; every value and span was transcribed cell by cell from the Markdown table and each span was checked to occur verbatim in the paper (grep). No TNFAIP3 variant is printed anywhere in the paper for any patient, so each of the 16 patients gets a variants row with variant_original_string 'not reported' (v3, D-22); no variant rows are made for the 15 relatives, whose variant status is nowhere stated. Labels: the paper's own IDs P3-P22 (Supplementary Table 1: 'The current ID of the patients is the same as the ID at the previous report (1).') and the relative IDs '<patient>-fa/-mo/-sib' ('P, patient; fa, Father; mo, mother; sib, sibling'). One relative, P8/P9-mo, is the mother of two patients and has one label. Relatives are in scope as relatives of patients ('Characteristics and microbiome diversity of the patients with HA20 and their relatives'); the paper calls them 'healthy family members' / 'healthy relatives'. Scope decisions: the study enrolled 18 patients, but only 16 (patients 3-5, 7-13, 17-22) appear in Supplementary Table 1; the remaining patients are mentioned only as counts and are not identifiable ('Clinical characteristics of the patients were previously reported (patients 3-5, 7-13, and 17-22)'), so they get no rows. The person called 'a sibling whose genetic information is unknown' and the healthy family members not listed in Supplementary Table 1 are mentioned only as counts/without any individual-level detail, so they get no rows either; they are counted in cohort_size_as_stated. is_proband is false for everyone (the paper calls no one a proband); no span is possible for a negative, so the span is null. Contradictions: the Results say 'Thirty-one fecal samples from 16 patients and 15 healthy family members were sequenced' while the abstract says 'Stool samples were obtained from 16 patients with HA20 and 15 of their family members'; the sample numbers analysed differ (13 vs 13) because samples were excluded. Checklist mapping: the item 'oral ulcers' is recorded from the Supplementary Table 1 column 'Stomatitis' (yes/no), the only oral finding; the paper never uses the word 'ulcer'. 'Abdominal symptoms' is recorded as a phenotypic feature only, never as 'gastrointestinal ulcers or inflammation', because the paper says 'not all patients with HA20 received gastrointestinal endoscopy, and so alternative indicators such as the disease severity or abdominal symptoms do not necessarily reflect the exact intestinal condition'. The column 'Antibiotics use from 6 months to 4 weeks ago' records antibiotic exposure, not infections, so it is not used for 'recurrent infections'. 'Nobody but an excluded younger brother (P22-sib) has food allergies' is treated as individual-level for P22-sib only, not as excluding food allergy for everyone else, because it does not name the group explicitly and its scope (participants vs analysed samples) is unclear. The '-' cells in the relatives' rows of Supplementary Table 1 (Severity, Stomatitis, Abdominal symptoms) are not defined as negative by the legend, so they are 'not reported' (v3, D-22); the legend defines only '*' (younger than 3 years) and the dagger (antibiotics within 4 weeks). Counts without names ('Eleven of 13 patients and eight of 13 presented with stomatitis and abdominal symptoms', 'four and five patients' with/without autoantibodies, 'Patients with HA20 consist of four mild, four moderate, and five severe patients') are never used to exclude a feature. Ages in Supplementary Table 1 are ages at stool-sample collection ('sex, age at the sample collection') and are recorded as age_at_last_evaluation; no age at onset or at diagnosis is given for anyone. disease_label_as_stated is left 'not reported' for the relatives, described only as 'healthy family members'; clinical_diagnosis_basis is 'not reported' for everyone (the diagnosis is not described). The separator ' / ' does not occur in any table of this paper, so D-31 raised no issue; the two stacked header blocks of Supplementary Table 2 (phylum counts) are used only to order the patients ('The healthy family members (upper) and patients (lower) are represented in order of age'). The Discussion sentence about 'one refractory patient [who] successfully received hematopoietic cell transplantation (Shiraki et al., 2021)' concerns a previously published person with no individual-level fact, so no row was created.",

6	"method_note": "Table transcription: Supplementary Table 1 (16 patients, 15 relatives) and the text were read directly; every value and span was transcribed cell by cell from the Markdown table and each span was checked to occur verbatim in the paper (grep). No TNFAIP3 variant is printed anywhere in the paper for any patient, so each of the 16 patients gets a variants row with variant_original_string 'not reported' (v3, D-22); no variant rows are made for the 15 relatives, whose variant status is nowhere stated. Labels: the paper's own IDs P3-P22 (Supplementary Table 1: 'The current ID of the patients is the same as the ID at the previous report (1).') and the relative IDs '<patient>-fa/-mo/-sib' ('P, patient; fa, Father; mo, mother; sib, sibling'). One relative, P8/P9-mo, is the mother of two patients and has one label. Relatives are in scope as relatives of patients ('Characteristics and microbiome diversity of the patients with HA20 and their relatives'); the paper calls them 'healthy family members' / 'healthy relatives'. Scope decisions: the study enrolled 18 patients, but only 16 (patients 3-5, 7-13, 17-22) appear in Supplementary Table 1; the remaining patients are mentioned only as counts and are not identifiable ('Clinical characteristics of the patients were previously reported (patients 3-5, 7-13, and 17-22)'), so they get no rows. The person called 'a sibling whose genetic information is unknown' and the healthy family members not listed in Supplementary Table 1 are mentioned only as counts/without any individual-level detail, so they get no rows either; they are counted in cohort_size_as_stated. is_proband is false for everyone (the paper calls no one a proband); no span is possible for a negative, so the span is null. Contradictions: the Results say 'Thirty-one fecal samples from 16 patients and 15 healthy family members were sequenced' while the abstract says 'Stool samples were obtained from 16 patients with HA20 and 15 of their family members'; the sample numbers analysed differ (13 vs 13) because samples were excluded. Checklist mapping: the item 'oral ulcers' is recorded from the Supplementary Table 1 column 'Stomatitis' (yes/no), the only oral finding; the paper never uses the word 'ulcer'. 'Abdominal symptoms' is recorded as a phenotypic feature only, never as 'gastrointestinal ulcers or inflammation', because the paper says 'not all patients with HA20 received gastrointestinal endoscopy, and so alternative indicators such as the disease severity or abdominal symptoms do not necessarily reflect the exact intestinal condition'. The column 'Antibiotics use from 6 months to 4 weeks ago' records antibiotic exposure, not infections, so it is not used for 'recurrent infections'. 'Nobody but an excluded younger brother (P22-sib) has food allergies' is treated as individual-level for P22-sib only, not as excluding food allergy for everyone else, because it does not name the group explicitly and its scope (participants vs analysed samples) is unclear. The '-' cells in the relatives' rows of Supplementary Table 1 (Severity, Stomatitis, Abdominal symptoms) are not defined as negative by the legend, so they are 'not reported' (v3, D-22); the legend defines only '*' (younger than 3 years) and the dagger (antibiotics within 4 weeks). Counts without names ('Eleven of 13 patients and eight of 13 presented with stomatitis and abdominal symptoms', 'four and five patients' with/without autoantibodies, 'Patients with HA20 consist of four mild, four moderate, and five severe patients') are never used to exclude a feature. Ages in Supplementary Table 1 are ages at stool-sample collection ('sex, age at the sample collection') and are recorded as age_at_last_evaluation; no age at onset or at diagnosis is given for anyone. disease_label_as_stated is left 'not reported' for the relatives, described only as 'healthy family members'; clinical_diagnosis_basis is 'not reported' for everyone (the diagnosis is not described). The separator ' / ' does not occur in any table of this paper, so D-31 raised no issue; the two stacked header blocks of Supplementary Table 2 (phylum counts) are used only to order the patients ('The healthy family members (upper) and patients (lower) are represented in order of age'). The Discussion sentence about 'one refractory patient [who] successfully received hematopoietic cell transplantation (Shiraki et al., 2021)' concerns a previously published person with no individual-level fact, so no row was created.",

6	"method_note": "Table transcription: Supplementary Table 1 (16 patients, 15 relatives) and the text were read directly; every value and span was transcribed cell by cell from the Markdown table and each span was checked to occur verbatim in the paper (grep). No TNFAIP3 variant is printed anywhere in the paper for any patient, so each of the 16 patients gets a variants row with variant_original_string 'not reported' (v3, D-22); no variant rows are made for the 15 relatives, whose variant status is nowhere stated. Labels: the paper's own IDs P3-P22 (Supplementary Table 1: 'The current ID of the patients is the same as the ID at the previous report (1).') and the relative IDs '<patient>-fa/-mo/-sib' ('P, patient; fa, Father; mo, mother; sib, sibling'). One relative, P8/P9-mo, is the mother of two patients and has one label. Relatives are in scope as relatives of patients ('Characteristics and microbiome diversity of the patients with HA20 and their relatives'); the paper calls them 'healthy family members' / 'healthy relatives'. Scope decisions: the study enrolled 18 patients, but only 16 (patients 3-5, 7-13, 17-22) appear in Supplementary Table 1; the remaining patients are mentioned only as counts and are not identifiable ('Clinical characteristics of the patients were previously reported (patients 3-5, 7-13, and 17-22)'), so they get no rows. The person called 'a sibling whose genetic information is unknown' and the healthy family members not listed in Supplementary Table 1 are mentioned only as counts/without any individual-level detail, so they get no rows either; they are counted in cohort_size_as_stated. is_proband is false for everyone (the paper calls no one a proband); no span is possible for a negative, so the span is null. Contradictions: the Results say 'Thirty-one fecal samples from 16 patients and 15 healthy family members were sequenced' while the abstract says 'Stool samples were obtained from 16 patients with HA20 and 15 of their family members'; the sample numbers analysed differ (13 vs 13) because samples were excluded. Checklist mapping: the item 'oral ulcers' is recorded from the Supplementary Table 1 column 'Stomatitis' (yes/no), the only oral finding; the paper never uses the word 'ulcer'. 'Abdominal symptoms' is recorded as a phenotypic feature only, never as 'gastrointestinal ulcers or inflammation', because the paper says 'not all patients with HA20 received gastrointestinal endoscopy, and so alternative indicators such as the disease severity or abdominal symptoms do not necessarily reflect the exact intestinal condition'. The column 'Antibiotics use from 6 months to 4 weeks ago' records antibiotic exposure, not infections, so it is not used for 'recurrent infections'. 'Nobody but an excluded younger brother (P22-sib) has food allergies' is treated as individual-level for P22-sib only, not as excluding food allergy for everyone else, because it does not name the group explicitly and its scope (participants vs analysed samples) is unclear. The '-' cells in the relatives' rows of Supplementary Table 1 (Severity, Stomatitis, Abdominal symptoms) are not defined as negative by the legend, so they are 'not reported' (v3, D-22); the legend defines only '*' (younger than 3 years) and the dagger (antibiotics within 4 weeks). Counts without names ('Eleven of 13 patients and eight of 13 presented with stomatitis and abdominal symptoms', 'four and five patients' with/without autoantibodies, 'Patients with HA20 consist of four mild, four moderate, and five severe patients') are never used to exclude a feature. Ages in Supplementary Table 1 are ages at stool-sample collection ('sex, age at the sample collection') and are recorded as age_at_last_evaluation; no age at onset or at diagnosis is given for anyone. disease_label_as_stated is left 'not reported' for the relatives, described only as 'healthy family members'; clinical_diagnosis_basis is 'not reported' for everyone (the diagnosis is not described). 12	IntroductionHaploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a form of inborn errors of immunity (IEI). IEIs are genetically occurring diseases, some of which cause intestinal dysbiosis. Due to the dysregulation of regulatory T cells (Tregs) observed in patients with HA20, gut dysbiosis was associated with Tregs in intestinal lamina propria.MethodsStool samples were obtained from 16 patients with HA20 and 15 of their family members. Infant samples and/or samples with recent antibiotics use were excluded; hence, 26 samples from 13 patients and 13 family members were analyzed. The 16S sequencing process was conducted to assess the microbial composition of samples. Combined with clinical information, the relationship between the microbiome and the disease activity was statistically analyzed.ResultsThe composition of gut microbiota in patients with HA20 was disturbed compared with that in healthy family members. Age, disease severity, and use of immunosuppressants corresponded to dysbiosis. However, other explanatory factors, such as abdominal symptoms and probiotic treatment, were not associated. The overall composition at the phylum level was stable, but some genera were significantly increased or decreased. Furthermore, among the seven operational taxonomic units (OTUs) that increased, two OTUs, Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus salivarius, considerably increased in patients with autoantibodies than those without autoantibodies.DiscussionDetailed interaction on intestinal epithelium remains unknown; the relationship between the disease and stool composition change helps us understand the mechanism of an immunological reaction to microorganisms.
40	Thirty-one fecal samples from 16 patients and 15 healthy family members were sequenced. However, samples from three patients who received antibiotic treatment within 4 weeks of stool collection were excluded from statistical analysis. Also, two samples from children under the age of 3 years were excluded from statistical analysis because their gut microbiome is naturally different from the older’s microbiome (Yatsunenko et al., 2012). Nobody but an excluded younger brother (P22-sib) has food allergies. The median (min–max) age of 13 patients with HA20 and their healthy family members of 13 individuals were 19 (3–43) and 36 (4–49) years (p = 0.09, Wilcoxon rank-sum test), respectively. Patients with HA20 consist of four mild, four moderate, and five severe patients. Eleven of 13 patients and eight of 13 presented with stomatitis and abdominal symptoms, respectively. One patient was treated with probiotics and 5 with immunosuppressants (Supplementary Table 1).
78	**Figure 3**: The composition of gut bacterial microbiota. The global composition of bacterial microbiota at the phylum level for the indicated groups. The healthy family members (left) and patients (middle) are represented in order of age. The two bars on the right are average values. P, patient; fa, Father; mo, mother; sib, sibling.
96	This study has several limitations. Firstly, clinical heterogeneity exists among medications, such as probiotics and antibiotics. The potential confounding factor is underestimated because of the small sample size. Secondly, because of rare diseases, it is difficult to collect more fecal samples for statistical analysis of the potential confounding factor described. Multivariate analysis was unfeasible due to small samples. Thirdly, not all patients with HA20 received gastrointestinal endoscopy, and so alternative indicators such as the disease severity or abdominal symptoms do not necessarily reflect the exact intestinal condition.

5	Journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology (2022)
6	Authors: Toyofuku Etsushi; Takeshita Kozue; Ohnishi Hidenori; Kiridoshi Yuko; Masuoka Hiroaki; Kadowaki Tomonori; Nishikomori Ryuta; Nishimura Kenichi; Kobayashi Chie; Ebato Takasuke; Shigemura Tomonari; Inoue Yuzaburo; Suda Wataru; Hattori Masahira; Morio Tomohiro; Honda Kenya; Kanegane Hirokazu
16	A20, which is encoded by the tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) gene, is a negative regulator of the TNF-nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway. Haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) causes autoinflammatory and autoimmune disorders (Kadowaki et al., 2018). Dysbiosis of the intestinal microbiome has been observed in some inborn errors of immunities (IEIs)/primary immunodeficiency disease, such as chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) (Sokol et al., 2016), X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis (XIAP) deficiency (Sokol et al., 2016; Ono et al., 2021), tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A (TTC7A) deficiency (Sokol et al., 2016), common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) (Jørgensen et al., 2016; Varricchi et al., 2021), and Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite IEIs having a monogenetic nature, they vary in severity relating to the microbiome (Liu et al., 2021). Little is known about the mechanism of dysbiosis in patients with IEI, but the association of gut microbiota and regulatory T cells (Tregs) was reported (Liu et al., 2021). Tregs regulate A20 (Kadowaki et al., 2020); as a result, the gut microbiota of patients with HA20 plays a vital role in association with Tregs. Alternatively, the mouse lacking A20 expression in dendritic cells showed intestinal dysbiosis (Talpin et al., 2019). This is the first report of the microbiome in patients with HA20.
22	Kadowaki et al. (2018) previously reported that there were 22 patients with HA20 from nine families in Japan. Thirty-six individuals from nine families, including 18 patients, 17 healthy family members living together, and a sibling whose genetic information is unknown, agreed to participate in this study. Next, fecal samples were obtained from 16 patients and 15 healthy relatives from eight corresponding families. Clinical characteristics of the patients were previously reported (patients 3–5, 7–13, and 17–22), and additional information, such as sex, age at the sample collection, symptoms, and medication, was collected (Supplementary Table 1).
